title: Zakat institutions
hook: mosques and charities collect and distribute zakat today

segments.voice: Yesterday, zakat and sadaqah, and your line: required and freely. One gift is measured and owed, the other open all day. Did your small sadaqah find its moment? Day one thousand one hundred four.

In the last days of Ramadan, a table goes up near the door of a mosque. There's a box, or a card reader, or a QR code taped to the wall, and a volunteer with a printed sheet of numbers. Somewhere else, a charity's website has a zakat calculator and a page that says where the money went last year. Neither the person paying nor the family receiving ever meets the other. So who carries the gift across? The Qur'an's own list of who receives zakat has an answer: it names the people who collect it. Today, zakat through many hands.
screen: `A TABLE BY THE MOSQUE DOOR.` → `A CALCULATOR ON A WEBSITE.` → `WHO CARRIES THE GIFT ACROSS?`

segments.voice: First, the collectors are in the text. Surah nine, verse sixty, lists the eight groups that zakat may go to, and among them, in Pickthall's words, is "those who collect them." Collecting and handing out zakat is work, and the Qur'an makes room to pay the people who do it from zakat itself. Second, in the text it is a task given to the Prophet himself. In surah nine, verse one hundred three, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told: "Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow." Those two words, purify and grow, are where this part of the path began. And when he sent Mu'adh ibn Jabal to Yemen, the report in Sahih al-Bukhari says he told him to teach the people that zakat is taken from their rich and given back to their poor. Their rich, their poor: some scholars read that as keeping zakat close to where it was collected. Third, today the hands look different from country to country. In some places a government agency collects zakat. In others it runs through a local mosque, a community fund, or a charity that works across borders. Scholars discuss questions these bodies face: whether zakat can go to a poor family far away when there is need nearby, and how much of it can pay for running costs. Different schools and scholars answer differently, and a good zakat charity will tell you which scholars it follows. Fourth, the giver's part. Giving through an institution isn't less personal; it can make the gift reach someone you'd never find alone. But the giver still has a job: to ask where it goes, and to trust the hands it passes through. That closes these days on zakat. A word for purifying and growing, a threshold, a year, eight doors, and a chain of people carrying a right to the one it belongs to.
screen: `THE COLLECTORS ARE IN 9:60.` · `TAKEN FROM THE RICH, GIVEN TO THE POOR.` · `MANY KINDS OF HANDS TODAY.` · `ASK WHERE IT GOES.` · then, large: `TAKE ALMS OF THEIR WEALTH, WHEREWITH THOU MAYST PURIFY THEM.`

segments.voice: The practice: look up a zakat charity, in your mind first and then for real. Settle, and breathe. Think about where help is needed that you care about: your own city, a place in the news, a place your family comes from. Hold that place for a minute. Then, after the bell, look up one organization that collects zakat for it, and find three things: who it serves, which scholars or school it follows, and what share goes to running costs. You don't have to give anything to do this. The bell holds the time.
Zakat institutions. The mosques, funds, agencies and charities that collect zakat and carry it to the people it belongs to; the Qur'an names the collectors among the eight. Today's word.

Your line: given through many hands. Today, thank one person whose job is to carry help to someone else. Tomorrow, a new pillar: the fast, and where it begins, in the heart, the night before. Day one thousand one hundred four.

howItsDone: Muslims pay zakat directly to people in need or through mosques, community funds, charities and, in some countries, government zakat agencies, which collect it and distribute it to the eight groups named in the Qur'an.

Sahih al-Bukhari: taken from their rich and given back to their poor.

fork.setup: a volunteer spends the last nights of Ramadan at the mosque table, collecting zakat and handing it out. can zakat itself pay for that work?
options: no; every coin must go straight to the poor.
yes; 9:60 names those who collect it among the eight.
only if the volunteer is poor too.
fork.reveal: yes. "those who collect them" are one of the eight groups in 9:60, so the work of carrying zakat can be paid from it.

original.note: Arabic, Qur'an 9:60: those who work on it, the collectors of zakat, named among its eight recipients.

trapdoor: what you thought: zakat is something you hand to a poor person yourself.
what it means: it can be, but the Qur'an also names collectors, and today mosques, funds and charities carry it.
what a scholar hears: al-'amilina 'alayha in 9:60; and the Mu'adh report, read by some schools as keeping zakat local where there is need.
